### ecs-awsvpc-eni-limits-tasks-per-instance

**Scope.** ECS tasks on Amazon EC2 Linux instances in awsvpc mode; the primary network interface counts as one toward the quota.

### ecs-bridge-mode-starts-faster-than-awsvpc-on-ec2

**Claim.** Tasks that use the bridge network mode on Amazon EC2 start faster than tasks that use the awsvpc network mode, because with awsvpc Amazon ECS attaches an ENI to the instance before launching the task; bridge tasks do not get their own security group.

**Write it as.** `start faster than tasks that use the `awsvpc`` · `These tasks don't get their own security group`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2.

> "Tasks that use `bridge` network mode on Amazon EC2 start faster than tasks that use the `awsvpc` network mode. When `awsvpc` network mode is used, Amazon ECS attaches an elastic network interface (ENI) to the instance before launching the task. This introduces additional latency. There are several tradeoffs for using bridge networking though. These tasks don't get their own security group, and there are some implications for load balancing."
> — [Amazon ECS capacity and availability](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-availability-best-practice.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-cluster-auto-scaling-reservation-above-or-below-target

**Claim.** When more tasks use a higher percentage of the capacity than the targetCapacity percentage, the increased CapacityProviderReservation metric causes its CloudWatch alarm to update the DesiredCapacity of the Auto Scaling group, and the group launches EC2 instances and registers them with the cluster; when fewer tasks use a lower percentage than targetCapacity and at least one instance can be terminated, the decreased metric causes the alarm to update DesiredCapacity, and the group terminates EC2 container instances and deregisters them from the cluster.

**Write it as.** `launch EC2 instances, and then register them` · `terminate EC2 container instances, and then deregister them`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS cluster auto scaling.

> "There are more tasks using a higher percentage of the capacity than your `targetCapacity` percentage. The increased value of the `CapacityProviderReservation` metric causes the associated CloudWatch alarm to act. This alarm updates the `DesiredCapacity` value for the Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group uses this value to launch EC2 instances, and then register them with the cluster."
> — [Automatically manage Amazon ECS capacity with cluster auto scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/cluster-auto-scaling.html)

> "There are fewer tasks using a lower percentage of the capacity than your `targetCapacity` percentage and there is at least one instance that can be terminated. The decreased value of the `CapacityProviderReservation` metric causes the associated CloudWatch alarm to act. This alarm updates the `DesiredCapacity` value for the Auto Scaling group. The Auto Scaling group uses this value to terminate EC2 container instances, and then deregister them from the cluster."
> — [Automatically manage Amazon ECS capacity with cluster auto scaling](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/cluster-auto-scaling.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

> "You must turn on Auto Scaling *instance scale-in protection* on the Auto Scaling group to use the managed termination protection feature of cluster auto scaling."
> — [Control the instances Amazon ECS terminates](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/managed-termination-protection.html)

> "Tasks that are run by a service that uses the `DAEMON` scheduling strategy are ignored and an instance can be terminated by cluster auto scaling even when the instance is running these tasks."

### ecs-task-is-instantiation-of-task-definition

**Claim.** A task is the instantiation of a task definition within a cluster, and after you create a task definition you can run it as a task or a service.

### ecs-task-role-credentials-exclusive-no-instance-inheritance

**Claim.** When you specify an IAM role for a task, the AWS CLI or SDKs in its containers use the credentials of the task role exclusively and do not inherit any IAM permissions from the EC2 or external instance they run on.

**Write it as.** `provided by the task role exclusively` · `do not inherit any IAM permissions`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task IAM role.

> "Note that when you specify an IAM role for a task, the AWS CLI or other SDKs in the containers for that task use the AWS credentials provided by the task role exclusively and they do not inherit any IAM permissions from the Amazon EC2 or external instance they are running on."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-task-role-fargate-no-instance-profile

**Claim.** On ECS Fargate, EC2 instance profiles are not available for containers in your tasks; task IAM roles let you associate IAM permissions with your containers irrespective of the compute option when you use the AWS SDK or AWS CLI in your containers, and CloudTrail logs show which task the role credentials were vended for.

**Write it as.** `EC2 instance profiles are not available` · `CloudTrail logs show which task`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task IAM role.

> "On ECS Fargate, EC2 instance profiles are not available for containers in your tasks. Task IAM roles enable you to associate IAM permissions to your containers irrespective of the compute option when you use AWS SDK or AWS CLI in your containers."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

> "Task credentials have a context of '`taskArn`' that is attached to the session, so CloudTrail logs show which task the role credentials were vended for."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-task-role-gives-app-code-aws-permissions

**Claim.** The ECS task IAM role allows application code running in the container to use other AWS services, such as Amazon S3; its permissions are vended to the containers in the task and are not accessed by the ECS container and Fargate agents.

**Write it as.** `allows your application code (running in the container)` · `aren't accessed by the Amazon ECS container`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task IAM role.

> "The permissions granted in the IAM role are vended to containers running in the task. This role allows your application code (running in the container) to use other AWS services. The task role is required when your application accesses other AWS services, such as Amazon S3."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

> "These permissions aren't accessed by the Amazon ECS container and Fargate agents."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-task-role-least-privilege-per-task-definition

**Claim.** If you have multiple task definitions or services that need IAM permissions, consider creating a role for each specific task definition or service with the minimum required permissions to minimize the access you provide to each task.

**Write it as.** `a role for each specific task definition` · `minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task IAM role.

> "If you have multiple task definitions or services that require IAM permissions, you should consider creating a role for each specific task definition or service with the minimum required permissions for the tasks to operate so that you can minimize the access that you provide for each task."
> — [Amazon ECS task IAM role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/task-iam-roles.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-task-size-load-test-for-requirements

**Claim.** Load testing your application is the key to successful resource requirement planning for ECS task sizes; a limit is the maximum CPU or memory a container or task can use, CPU above the limit is throttled and memory above the limit stops the container.

**Write it as.** `Load testing your application is the key` · `your container being stopped`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task sizing.

> "A limit is the maximum amount of CPU units or memory that your container or task can use. Any attempt to use more CPU more than this limit results in throttling. Any attempt to use more memory results in your container being stopped."
> — [Best practices for Amazon ECS task sizes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-tasksize.html)

> "Load testing your application is the key to successful resource requirement planning and better understanding your application's requirements."
> — [Best practices for Amazon ECS task sizes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-tasksize.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-task-size-stateless-small-reservations-cost

**Claim.** For stateless applications that scale horizontally, smaller CPU reservations such as 256 CPU units (1/4 vCPU) scale out in a fine-grained way that minimizes cost but might not scale fast enough for big spikes, while larger CPU reservations scale faster but cost more.

**Write it as.** `a fine-grained way that minimizes cost` · `larger CPU reservations are more costly`

**Scope.** Amazon ECS task sizing.

> "You can use smaller CPU reservations, such as 256 CPU units (or 1/4 vCPU), to scale out in a fine-grained way that minimizes cost. But, they might not scale fast enough to meet significant spikes in demand. You can use larger CPU reservations to scale in and out more quickly and therefore match demand spikes more quickly. However, larger CPU reservations are more costly."
> — [Best practices for Amazon ECS task sizes](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/capacity-tasksize.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.

### ecs-tasks-per-service-limit

**Claim.** One ECS service can have at most 5,000 tasks (the desired count) in each supported Region, and the quota is not adjustable; services configured to use Amazon ECS service discovery have a limit of 1,000 tasks per service because of the AWS Cloud Map service quota.

**Write it as.** `5,000 tasks` · `1,000 tasks per service`

**Scope.** per service, per Region; maximum; not adjustable.

> "Tasks per service | Each supported Region: 5,000 | No | The maximum number of tasks per service (the desired count)." (columns: Name | Default | Adjustable | Description)
> — [Amazon ECS endpoints and quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/ecs-service.html)

> "Services configured to use Amazon ECS service discovery have a limit of 1,000 tasks per service. This is due to the AWS Cloud Map service quota for the number of instances per service."
> — [Amazon ECS endpoints and quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/ecs-service.html)

**Checked.** 2026-10-14.
